You're just telling me what to build. That sucks. I don't want that kind of work." So, is the solution to that the engineering lead was super involved and detailed, and the design lead was super involved, and so you can trust that you're not just the code monkey building the thing they told you to build?
turns.zh: 本期节目由Airtable ProductCentral赞助。这是一个统一的系统，能将你的整个产品团队整合在一个平台上。再也不用在不同工具间切换，也不用让团队目标偏离。和大多数产品负责人一样，你厌倦了在不同工具间频繁切换上下文。这就是Airtable与世界级产品公司合作数十年后打造ProductCentral的原因。可以把它看作是整个产品组织的指挥中心。与僵化的点解决方案不同，ProductCentral涵盖从资源调配到客户反馈、路线图制定再到发布执行的全过程。基于Airtable无代码平台，你可以完全自定义工作流程，使其与团队工作方式无缝契合。没有限制，没有妥协。想亲眼见证？访问airtable.com/lenny即可预约演示。（00:46:58）：你提到的，我想很多听众会想，“天哪，我真不敢这么做。”如果描述得太详细，团队里的工程师和设计师就会说：“搞什么鬼？你就是在告诉我们要做什么，这太糟糕了。我不想做这种工作。”那么解决办法是不是工程负责人要深度参与，设计负责人也要深度参与，这样才能确保大家不会只是按照别人告诉的去建模型？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: That's really interesting. I got to tell you, the dominant failure case that I see in the real world is always, again and again, not enough detail. And it's also the most common failure mode where the engineers run back to the product folks and say, "I'm not getting enough from you." It is really like that, but I can understand why the hair stands up on the back of the neck a little bit thinking about it because, of course, if you give a senior engineer like, "Here's how I want you to go implement the schema for this database change for this model," they're going to be like, "What do you think? Who are you? Who are you?" You know what I mean? But what's really interesting is it's not a universal thing. The amount of detail that the team is going to feel helps them is a dial that we can turn that depends on who's on the team. (00:48:28): So, if you have a more junior person who's on the build team and then you have a more senior engineer who's involved in the shaping, they can make that junior engineer much more successful with additional detail. So, we're going to do this and I would suggest approaching it like this, this, this, and this. That junior person is, when they don't know how to do it, they're not going to ask because they don't want to show that they don't know, and they're going to hide the fact that they're lost and it's going to blow up later in the project. And on the other hand, if they are given more guidance, they're going to be able to be successful. They're going to learn about this is how this person who knows well, kind of approached it and then in the next round or a few projects later, you can dial it back and say, "Well, let's give less detail and see how they handle it." (00:49:19): So, you can really give people bigger shoes to grow into and help them to be successful. And then, of course, you can also do it the other way around where if you've got some really stellar talent on the team and you have a long history and you have a lot of trust that they are going to be able to understand and solve it, then of course, you can leave things out. (00:49:40): But the thing that I often see is if there's someone on the build team who really feels that they should be involved in the fundamental decisions about the approach, then a better solution would be to actually bring them into the shaping and have them play that technical role in the shaping session. If they have the right skills and the right perspective and the right knowledge to play that role well, then just bring them into the shaping. So, it's all about how do we bring people into a moment where we are using their strengths and then we're giving them an input, so that whatever their work step is that they're able to apply the maximum creativity, but also have the maximum clarity, so that they can really use that time well and also feel good about what they're doing.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。我得跟你说，我在现实世界中见过的最常见的失败案例，往往是因为细节不足。这也是工程师们最常抱怨的情况——他们会跑去找产品团队说：“你们给我的信息太少了！”确实如此，但一想到这点，你难免会后背发凉，因为如果给一个资深工程师说：“我希望你按照这个方案去实现数据库的更改”，他们很可能会反问：“你觉得我行？你是谁啊？” 你懂我的意思吧？但有趣的是，这并非普遍现象。团队需要的详细程度是可以调节的，这取决于团队成员的资质。（00:48:28）比如，如果构建团队中有经验较浅的成员，而参与设计的工程师经验更丰富，那么额外的指导就能让这些初级工程师更容易成功。这样做的好处是，当他们遇到难题时，会主动寻求帮助，而不是藏着掖着假装懂，避免项目后期出现问题。而如果给予他们更多指导，他们就能成功。通过观察资深工程师的处理方式，他们能学到新方法。几轮项目之后，再逐渐减少指导，让他们自主应对。（00:49:19）这样就能给他们成长的空间，助力他们成功。当然，反之亦然——如果团队中有极具天赋的成员，且双方长期合作互信，那么可以适当放权。（00:49:40）但我常发现，如果构建团队中有成员觉得自己应该参与核心决策阶段，最好的解决方案就是让他们参与设计环节，在设计会上发挥技术作用。只要他们具备相应技能、视角和知识，就能胜任这一角色。关键在于如何让团队成员发挥优势，提供清晰指导，让他们在每个工作环节都能最大限度地发挥创造力和清晰度，充分利用时间，并从工作中获得满足感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like the core of this is de-risk the biggest risks and address the biggest unknowns as much as possible. There's probably this 80% of here are the risks. Let's just understand them deeply before we commit to this appetite.
turns.zh: 核心问题似乎在于尽可能降低最大风险，解决最不确定的因素。这里可能有80%的风险。让我们先深入理解这些风险，再投入精力应对。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: That is exactly right. There are these, we can call them rabbit holes, we can call them time bombs. There are these things where we say, "Oh, it'll be fine." One example, simple example, I worked with a team and they had a step of onboarding in a FinTech product and there was this step of onboarding and they would lose a lot of people in the funnel at that step because you had to fill out a whole bunch of information, and they figured out that they could actually pipe that data in from one of the partners that they had. They were partnered with banks and they're like, "Oh, we don't even need to be asking people this. So, we're going to fix conversion. We're going to eliminate a step from our user experience. It's going to be great." (00:51:26): The thing that they didn't look at was if you go into the code on that step of the onboarding, it's not actually one step. There's like three different branches of that step depending on which bank the customer is integrated on. And so, that's the kind of thing where it all sounds so great and simple, and then you get into the weeds and you realize like, "Oh, wait a minute." You know what I mean? So, now, we have decisions to make. Now, if you're in the middle of a project and it's already been resourced and people are already on the hook that we're supposed to be doing this, and you already got the alignment that the engineering time is happening for this, and you're finding that out in week four. You know what I mean? You did all these beautiful drawings, by the way, and now, you're finding this out in week four, that's a bad place to be. (00:52:14): But if we're in the shaping room and we didn't kick this thing off yet, we didn't even green light the project yet, and we have an engineer there, not just the product people, not just the designer, but we have that engineer who really insists on sometimes, I like to think of it like the grumpy old plumber who's seen everything and he insists on opening up the walls and looking at the pipes before he'll give you a quote. So, it's like when you've got that person in the room, they're saying, "Yeah, that all sounds great. Let's take a quick look at the code and figure out what screen you're actually talking about. Just let's just take a quick look." And it only takes a moment to open up the code, find this thing that we're talking about, and really look at it and say, "Oh, it's more complicated than we thought." (00:52:59): And now, it's not like, "Okay, now, we're screwed and the project is going to be bigger." Now, we can have a really cool conversation about trade-offs. So, let's say we've got three different integrations here, three different segments integrated into different banks. How big are they relative to each other in terms of the deals we made or the percentage of customers who flow through those three different conditions? If we just did this on one of those branches, would it be a win? And if we did it on all three, how much more time would we have to negotiate for and would it feel worth it? You see, we're getting into this horse-trading of what is important, what's worth it, what do we need to get out of it? And that's really productive. And when you're doing that before the project starts off, that feels like, "Oh, we're talking about the important things. We're not failing right now. We are engaged in the hard questions that are going to enable us to really ship something that's successful later."
turns.zh:
确实如此。有些情况我们称之为"兔子洞"、"定时炸弹"。有些时候我们会想，"哦，应该没问题的。"举个简单的例子，我曾与一个团队合作，他们在金融科技产品中设计了一个用户注册流程，但在这一步就流失了大量用户，因为用户需要填写大量信息。后来他们发现，可以从合作的银行直接导入数据，于是决定取消这一步骤，简化用户体验。听起来很棒，但深入研究后发现，这个流程实际上有三个分支，取决于用户关联的银行不同。这种看似简单易行的方案，实则暗藏玄机。  

当项目已进入实施阶段，资源投入已定，工程时间表也已敲定，却在第四周才发现问题，这时再想调整就难上加难了。（00:51:26） 好在如果我们还在项目策划阶段，还没启动项目，甚至还没获得最终批准，团队里有工程师参与（不只是产品经理和设计师），他们会坚持亲自检查代码。比如那个脾气暴躁的老水管工，见多识广，坚持要先拆墙看管道。这时工程师会说："嗯，听起来不错。但我们先快速看看代码，确认具体是哪个页面。"只需几分钟就能定位问题所在，发现实际情况比想象复杂得多。  

（00:52:14） 接下来就不是"完蛋了，项目要延期了"，而是开启一场高效的权衡讨论。假设有三个不同的银行接口，每个分支都需要单独处理。三者在交易量和客户转化率上差异巨大。如果只处理其中一个分支，是否足够？处理全部三个分支，又需要额外投入多少时间？是否值得？这时候我们需要评估优先级，权衡利弊。  

（00:52:59） 这种前置的探讨能避免项目偏离轨道，真正让团队专注于核心问题。当项目尚在策划阶段时，我们就能进行有效的博弈：哪个分支更关键？各分支的客户转化率如何？如果只处理其中一个，是否足够？处理全部三个分支，又值得吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let's go one level deeper on this shaping session, because clearly, that is so core to this working, and I know you have a whole book about how to actually do this. So, we're not going to-
turns.zh: 好的，让我们再深入探讨一下这次塑形会议，因为显然这对我们的工作至关重要，而且我知道你有一整本关于如何具体操作的书。所以，我们不打算——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... to this working, and I know you have a whole book about how to actually do this, so we're not going to answer all the questions, and there's a lot of detail and nuance. But a few questions, how long do these usually take? It sounds like a whole day experience, and then it sounds like you invite as few people as possible, but not too few people. What's your guidance on who should join?
turns.zh: ……深入探讨这次工作，我知道你有一整本关于如何具体操作的书，所以我们不打算回答所有问题，其中有很多细节和微妙之处。但还是要回答几个问题：这些会议通常持续多久？听起来像是一整天的体验，然后你们邀请的人数尽可能少，但又不能太少。对于谁应该参加，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: In this shaping and real life course, we've been doing workshops where we try to help people to learn what it's like in a shaping session. One of the things that's always interesting to me is how... So Kathy and I will be running the session and we have to... People aren't used to working so fast. What are we actually doing right now? What's the decision? What's an idea right now? We're not going to go away and draw something, and then I'll comment on a document and then come back and get together tomorrow. What ideas do we actually have right now starting from zero? So imagine, we've narrowed down the calendar problem too. It's about empty spaces. We are willing, from a business standpoint, to spend six weeks on a whack at this where it's solved. We believe there's a way that's possible, so what can we come up with?
turns.zh: 在这次塑形与现实生活课程中，我们一直在举办研讨会，试图帮助人们了解塑形会议的运作方式。其中让我一直感兴趣的一点是……所以凯西和我将主持这次会议，我们必须……人们不习惯这么快地工作。我们现在到底在做什么？现在该做什么决定？现在有什么想法？我们不会先去画点什么，然后我在文档里评论，再明天回来开会。我们现在从零开始，到底有什么想法？想象一下，我们已经把日历问题缩小到空白部分。从商业角度来看，我们愿意花六周时间全力攻克这个问题，直到解决。我们相信有可行的方法，那我们能想出什么办法呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's the input to the framing session or sorry, the shaping session.
turns.zh: 以上就是塑形会议（或者说抱歉，是塑形研讨会）的输入内容。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Exactly. Having a narrowed down problem from the framing work, and this is a whole other topic of very often the PMs are sometimes just taking something at face value and not negotiating down to really narrow down what is this really, and where is the value in this? But let's suppose that that's happened, that we've narrowed down the problem, so now we've got a narrow problem. So now what we need to do is try out different ideas, and this is the real thing. We have to try to break them. So I want to draw an idea, and then I want the technical person to find, oh, this isn't going to... You know what I mean? This isn't going to work because of this reason. Or the product person is going to be looking in and saying, "I get that that's really an easy way to do it technically, but I don't think that we're actually delivering the value if I play through the customer scenario here." You know what I mean? (00:56:24): So there's these different angles where the idea can fail, and one of the things that we also coach people to do in a session is not just to go down one path and then be stuck in one idea and now you're going in circles around little details of one idea for three hours, but to really step back and say, "Here's an approach. What if we had the scrolling agenda view, okay? And that's idea A. Then what's a very different way of doing this?" Do you know what I mean? If we didn't want to have the agenda view there, is there a way to do this where it's just a month view? Let's see if we can draw that. So that's the thing that's happening. You asked about the time, and I started with people aren't used to just going all the way in to actually trying ideas. (00:57:16): So there is a little bit of learning how to just face that blank page and start trying things together. What we find is that a three-hour session can be very, very productive to help you figure out what do we already have that are possible approaches to this? What are some major missing things? Like, okay, I've got the calendar dot grid, I've got the agenda idea, but what about multi-day events? Do you know what I mean? So there can be these things, these what abouts. So then maybe we break and we think for a little bit, and somebody sketches some ideas on that and does a spike or two on something, and we come back again for another three hours or we come back the next day. And what I would say is if the project that you're trying to do is doable with, let's say, your existing technology, you're not inventing a new algorithm, you're not inventing some new database or... You know what I mean? (00:58:25): You're not doing a new AI model. It's more about how do I use the APIs and the frameworks and the tech stack that we have? How do I put that together to build something? Then if the problem is clear and the time is now, you will be able to come to a conclusion about what's possible to build in three sessions, something like that. The key thing is leaning into those sessions and really wrestling with each other. If you have just the product and the designer there and then it's like, well, we'll show this to the technical person later, then it can all blow up. And then you find out it's more complicated than you thought and you have to go back to the drawing board. We need to have all the necessary information in the same room for these sessions to go fast.
turns.zh:
没错。通过前期框架工作，我们已经把问题缩小到了一个具体范围，但这完全是另一个话题——很多项目经理往往会想当然地接受现有方案，而不深入探讨问题的本质：这项功能的真正价值在哪里？不过假设问题已经明确了，接下来我们需要测试各种方案，这才是关键所在。我们必须打破常规思维。比如我要提出一个想法，然后让技术人员分析：“哦，这个方案行不通，因为存在这样那样的问题。”或者产品经理会反驳：“虽然技术上可以实现，但从用户场景来看，这并不能创造真正的价值。”明白我的意思吗？（00:56:24）  
在这些会议中，想法很容易陷入死胡同。比如大家只专注于一个方向，却在某个细节上反复纠缠三小时。这时候就需要后退一步，重新思考：“我们可以尝试这种方法。假设采用滚动日程视图，怎么样？这是方案A。那有没有完全不同的实现方式？”比如，如果不想用日程视图，能否用月视图替代？我们可以画出原型图，进行验证。  
正如你所问的，时间管理至关重要。但关键在于，人们不习惯直接动手尝试新方案。（00:57:16）  
所以需要逐步培养这种直面空白页面、共同探索的能力。通过三小时的头脑风暴，我们能清晰了解现有资源中的潜在方案，以及尚存的关键缺失点。比如用户提到的多日活动场景，技术团队可能需要补充相关功能。  
总之，关键在于利用现有技术堆栈，快速验证可行性。比如避免发明新算法、新数据库等复杂模块，而是专注于如何整合现有API、框架和技术栈。只要问题清晰、时机成熟，三小时内就能得出可行的方案。  
核心在于全员参与，激烈碰撞。若只有产品和设计师参与，后续又让技术人员审核，整个过程可能崩盘。所有关键角色必须齐聚一堂，才能高效推进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so much genius built into this approach, and it sits on top of human nature. One is just, you need to actually spend... go into the deep edge cases and nuances and not just-
turns.zh: 这种方法中蕴含着诸多巧思，而且它顺应了人类的天性。关键在于，你需要真正投入精力——深入研究各种极端场景和细微差别，而不只是敷衍了事。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's fine. Let's go with [inaudible 00:59:34].
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。我们就按[不可听清00:59:34]来吧。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: More concreteness.
turns.zh: 要更具体些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very concrete, very in depth, and then the appetites are... There's just so many elements of this that just connect with the way humans work versus the theory of just like, "Yeah. Well, let's see how long this will take. It'll be a great... and we'll figure it out as we're building. We don't need to really figure this out. Yeah. We don't have time for that."
turns.zh: 非常具体、深入，而用户需求——这里有太多元素与人类的工作方式相契合，而不是那种只说"嗯，先看看要花多长时间，再看看效果如何"的理论派。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: And we're solving a puzzle together, if it needs to be doable in this amount of time. But it also has to hit these points in terms of the problem we're solving. You know what I mean? It has to do these things, but in this time. One other thing that I would mention is that we can't be drawing Figma files. By the way, I'm being very mean to Figma so far in this conversation. There is a time when it's the right time for the Figma file. What we want to do is have that clarity around the... Let's say, we already know where the sink is going in the kitchen and now we can make final calls about the tile and the exact fixture-
turns.zh: 我们是在一起解谜，如果要在既定时间内完成任务。但同时也必须在解决问题的核心要点上达成共识。你懂我的意思吧？必须完成这些任务，同时还要在既定时间内完成。另外，我要提到的是，我们不能一直画Figma文件。说实话，在这次讨论中我对Figma挺刻薄的。但Figma确实有它适用的场景。比如说，我们已经确定了厨房水槽的位置，现在可以敲定瓷砖和固定装置的具体方案——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Grout color.
turns.zh: 勾缝颜色。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: ... and stuff like that. Right, grout color. We don't want to have to throw it all away every time something changes. So there's a time and a place where Figma is amazing and feels good and it's like, oh, now it's beautiful. Now, it's amazing. But in a shaping session, you can't collaborate on something so high fidelity. So we need also some ways to collaborate, and this is where you see these techniques in the book, like breadboarding and fat marker sketching. These are tools to help us express an idea very, very clearly in detail. We're going to hit this button and from this button, go to here. This calculation runs, then we get this answer, and then we have this choice to go here or here. That's the thing that we need to be seeing and that's the level of detail where we can move fast together but still see something real as more this breadboarding level.
turns.zh: ……诸如此类的事情。对吧，就是勾缝颜色。我们不想每次有改动就把所有成果推倒重来。所以Figma有它存在的时机和地点，我们需要它来展示美观的界面。但在设计阶段，你无法进行如此高保真度的协作。因此，我们还需要其他协作方式，这就是书中提到的技术，比如原型搭建和胖马克笔速写。这些工具能帮助我们非常清晰地表达设计思路。我们点击这个按钮，从这里跳到那里。计算结果出来，然后我们可以选择去这里或那里。这才是我们需要关注的细节层次，既能快速推进，又能让大家看到真实的东西——更接近原型搭建的水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fat marker session is very evocative of what this whole session is about, is very high level sketches. That's a great term.
turns.zh: 胖马克笔速写很好地传达了整个设计过程的精髓，是一种高层次的草图。这真是个绝妙的术语。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: The danger there that I often see is that what we don't want is to say, "Oh, Figma isn't the right thing at this level. So instead, we're going to do fat marker sketches," and what you get is the equivalent of a blurry Figma. Do you know what I mean? Just less detailed. What we need from a fat marker sketch for it to be valuable to us as builders is it has to really communicate the idea. When I look at that, I'm like, "Oh, now I get it?" And if it's more this general wire frame of dashboard goes here and there's going to be four reports, and it's like I still don't know what to build, right?
turns.zh: 但我经常看到的一个问题是，我们不应简单地说“Figma在当前阶段不合适，所以我们改用胖马克笔速写”，结果得到的只是模糊的Figma效果。懂我的意思吧？就是不够详细。我们需要胖马克笔速写为我们这些开发者带来价值，它必须能清晰传达设计理念。当我看到这样的成果时，我会想“哦，现在我明白了？”但如果只是一个通用的仪表板框架，四个报告之类的，我还是不知道该怎么做，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: So if it's not telling me what to build, so maybe this is a way to come back to your question about what's the output of the shaping session, it's like it's shaped if we can give this to a technical person and they say, "Yeah, I know what to go build now."
turns.zh: 好，如果它没有告诉我该建什么东西，也许这就是回到你关于塑形会议产出的问题的一种方式。就是说，如果我们把这份成果交给技术人员，他们会说：“是的，我现在知道该去建什么了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm very happy with our overview of the process. I think we've done a really good job giving people the gist. And obviously, if they want to actually implement it, they can get the book and dive in or work with you, which we'll point people to. Say someone's like, "This is awesome. I want to do this." What would you say is a good first step for a team that's currently... let's say, they're in startup land, and they're just shipping every two weeks, maybe every week? So maybe for that bucket of folks and then also for a larger company, I don't know, Agile Scrum SAFe, and they're just like, "Oh, let's try something different."
turns.zh: 我对我们对这个过程的概述非常满意。我认为我们在向人们传达核心要义方面做得很棒。显然，如果他们想实际应用它，可以去读这本书，或者与你们团队合作——我们会为他们指明方向。比如有人会说：“这太棒了。我想这么做。”你会怎么建议一个目前处于创业阶段的团队？比如，他们每两周或每周发布一次版本。还有大公司，比如敏捷、Scrum、SAFe，他们可能也想尝试些新东西。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Sometimes dev teams, they like the idea of not having the Scrum ritual, so they want to take in the six weeks, but unless the engineering and product come together to figure out how to collaboratively shape, like we talked about before, that time box isn't going to go well. So I-
turns.zh: 有时候开发团队喜欢不遵循Scrum仪式，所以他们想延长六周的周期，但除非工程和产品团队能共同协作进行塑形（就像我们之前讨论的），那样的时间框架很难顺利推进。所以我-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They think they're going to not have to do standups, but now it's a day of hard thinking.
turns.zh: 他们以为不用开站会了，但现在却变成了漫长的一天用来艰难思考。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Well, it turns into even more meetings, because we don't know what to do.
turns.zh: 嗯，会议反而更多了，因为我们不知道该做什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the more meetings is just that shaping session specifically. Right?
turns.zh: 而更多的会议就集中在塑形环节上，对吧？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: No, what I mean is that if we didn't-
turns.zh: 不，我是说如果我们只采用六周周期，却不进行塑形，那我们就不知道该做什么了。然后到了期限，我们基本上只能边做边塑形。然后时间不够了，最后感觉这根本算不上……虽然能从Scrum仪式中解脱出来很不错，但我们不能再一次又一次地庆祝发布成功之类的。对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, right. I [inaudible 01:03:46] right.
turns.zh: 这确实是个好时机，也许可以谈谈Scrum中的春季启动仪式。人们可能觉得这和春季启动仪式差不多。但其实-

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: If we only adopted the six-week cycle and said we're going to figure it out and we didn't adopt the shaping, then we just don't know what to do. And then we reached the end, and we're basically scrambling to shape it as we go. And then we run out of time, and then we feel like this wasn't... It was nice to get a break from the Scrum rituals, but we can't say that we are knocking the champagne bottle on the boat because we're celebrating the launch or whatever, again and again. Right?
turns.zh: 哦，这主意不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good, actually, time to maybe talk about there's obviously the spring kickoff in Scrum. What's main difference for people, because they may be thinking, "Oh, this is just like a spring kickoff." That's-
turns.zh: 确实是个好机会。所以在Scrum团队中，通常会有人创建这些任务清单，列出冲刺阶段要做的事情。但在我看来，很多情况下，这些任务清单不是由实际开发的人创建的。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Oh, that's a good one.
turns.zh: 对，就是产品负责人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... big deal.
turns.zh: ……这很重要。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: That's a good one. So what you often see in a Scrum team is that there's somebody who creates these tickets of these are the things that are going to happen inside of the sprint. Really, in my opinion, too many cases, it's not the person who's doing the building who's creating those tickets.
turns.zh: 这主意不错。所以在Scrum团队中，通常会有人创建这些任务清单，列出冲刺阶段要做的事情。但在我看来，很多情况下，这些任务清单不是由实际开发的人创建的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your product owner.
turns.zh: 所以是产品负责人。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: So there's a big, big gap there. We could talk a lot about that, but there's gaps in context. The person who's writing the ticket doesn't actually understand the work that's involved. You know what I mean? So there are so many unknowns and time bombs waiting in those tickets that sound reasonable, but they weren't really created by the person who understands the work that needs to happen. So the key difference is two things. So in Scrum, you have a person who's not the builders making tickets, and this is what in the cruel picture is the paper shredder. In the shape-up world, you have a single idea that was shaped. This is the thing we shaped with the two months in the agenda view and da da. Go make your own tasks, because you're the professionals. Do you know what I mean? So the contractors, if you're building a house, they have to know the plans, but you don't have to tell them, "Now take the hammer and go over here." (01:05:52): That's their, right? So in a shape-up world, a kickoff is, here's the well-shaped idea, and now this time box starts. At Basecamp, it was really, really loose because they are just stocked with senior people. They have so many very senior engineers and all the designers are coding. They're very technical, really, really skilled people. What I found is helpful when the team is a little bit more mixed, if they're not all super senior, is a simple exercise of at kickoff, take whatever was shaped and just draw a grid with nine boxes, and give me nine boxes of the nine major chunks that you think have to get implemented from an implementation standpoint. So translate this into nine major scopes of implementation that need to somehow happen over the time box. So really, really useful exercise to kick things off, and we have a lot of teams doing that now. (01:06:52): If you take six weeks, that's 30 business days. You divide that by nine, it's four days per box. So you're going to get a lot of clarity from a quick exercise. And again, this is done by the builders. This is a really also good exercise for them to notice like, "Oh, wait a minute, we think there's too much scope here. Even though it seemed reasonable, when we put it into nine boxes, it's like, I don't think we can do this all." Or it's also a good moment where somebody who's more junior might describe their implementation approach, and then someone who's senior can review that and say, "Actually, we've done that before, and we'll run into this trouble if we don't use this other thing." So those really nice coaching moments can happen.
turns.zh: 所以这里存在着巨大的、巨大的差距。我们可以对此展开诸多讨论，但存在着背景信息的缺失。开罚单的人实际上并不了解相关工作的具体内容。你懂我的意思吧？所以有很多未知数和定时炸弹潜藏在那些看似合理的工单里，但它们并非由真正理解所需工作的团队成员创建的。关键的区别在于两点。在Scrum中，开罚单的人并非实际的执行者，这在残酷的图景中就如同碎纸机。而在Shape Up世界里，团队会形成一个经过充分塑形的想法。这就是我们用两个月的日程视图塑形出来的成果，然后你们就可以自行分配任务了，因为你们是专业人士。你懂我的意思吧？比如说，如果你在建房子，承包商必须了解设计图，但你不必对他们说：“现在拿起锤子去那边干活。”（01:05:52）：这就是他们的职责，对吧？所以在Shape Up世界里，启动会就是这样：这里是经过充分塑形的想法，现在时间框开始了。在Basecamp，流程非常松散，因为那里都是资深员工。他们有很多资深工程师，设计师也都在写代码。他们都是技术能力非常强、技能高超的人。我发现，当团队成员结构更复杂、并非全是资深人才时，一个简单的练习很有帮助。在启动会上，拿出经过塑形的想法，画出一个包含九个方格的网格，然后让团队成员分别列出从实施角度来看必须完成的九个主要部分。这确实是一个非常有效的启动方式，现在很多团队都在这样做。（01:06:52）：如果给六周时间，那就是30个工作日。除以9，每个方格对应四天。所以通过这个快速练习，你能清晰了解整体情况。这同样是由执行者完成的。这也是一个很好的指导时刻，让他们意识到：“哦，等等，我们觉得范围太大了。即使看起来合理，但把它分成九个部分后，我们觉得根本做不完。”或者这也是一个很好的时刻，让初级成员描述他们的实施方法，然后资深成员可以审视并说：“实际上，我们之前做过类似的，如果不采用其他方法，就会遇到这个问题。”所以这些非常好的指导时刻就能出现了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you were to try this approach and have a shaping session, this is a sign you're heading in a good direction, is if the output, the team that's building it can come up with nine... Does it have to be nine? Is six cool, 10 cool?
turns.zh: 如果你尝试这种方法并进行塑形会议，那么一个好的迹象就是，团队能够列出九个……必须是九个吗？六个可以吗？十个也可以吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: What I found is if it's more than 10, then you just get into ticket land of, here's a million things I have to do. You know what I mean? If you have 100 things, that doesn't tell me anything. But if it has to be nine or less.
turns.zh: 我发现，如果超过10个，那你就会陷入工单的困境，比如这里有无数的事情要做。你懂我的意思吧？如果你有100个任务，那说明不了什么。但如果必须是九个或更少。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nine or less. Okay. Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 九个或更少。好的。好的，不错。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: I actually think... I'm speculating here, but the UX designers in your audience will know about this rule of seven, plus or minus two. It's this cognitive science principle that was found about how many things someone can hold in their head at once. So this nine is the upper limit of seven plus or minus two, and it basically... It's like, do we actually have a picture of what it means to build this that we can also hold in our heads? Can we see the whole castle?
turns.zh: 实际上我觉得……我这只是猜测，但听众中的用户体验设计师应该都听说过“七加减二”这个规则。这是认知科学领域的一个原理，指的是人们一次能在脑中同时处理的事物数量。因此，九个元素刚好是七加减二的上限。关键在于……我们能否构想出一个清晰的解决方案，让大家都能轻松理解？比如说，我们能否直观地呈现整个“城堡”的全貌？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing is if you're on a, say, Agile Scrum team today, if you want to start trying this out, it's schedule a shaping session, assume it's six weeks to start, try to come into it with a framing of here's the problem we're trying to solve. Is that a good way of thinking about it, like the problem we're trying to solve?
turns.zh: 所以我的理解是，如果你现在在一个敏捷Scrum团队中，想尝试这种方法，可以先安排一次“塑形会议”。假设项目周期为六周，首先要明确我们要解决的问题。这是否是一个合理的思考方式？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah, for sure. The question is what problem are we trying to solve, because the shaping work is more what are our options for the solution? And if the problem is too fuzzy and big, if the problem is just calendar, then the shaping is going to be this ever-expanding, never-ending thing, and we're not going to be able to get anywhere.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。关键问题在于我们要解决什么样的问题？因为塑形阶段更多的是去探索解决方案的可能性。如果问题过于模糊、过于宏大，比如只是一个日程管理的问题，那么塑形阶段就会变成一个不断扩展、永无止境的过程，最终一事无成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. So you spend three hours, maybe six hours in the first session. Would you recommend try to keep it to this many hours when you're first trying it up?
turns.zh: 是的。好的。那么第一次会议可能需要三到六个小时。你建议第一次尝试时，时长最好控制在多少小时以内？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: No, I wouldn't do that. I think the key thing is actually if you get to the point where you're trying to hold a shaping session and you manage to get product and engineering into the same room to do it, you are far along. You're doing great if you're at that point. Oh, so much of the challenge is getting to the point of aligning between product and engineering that we cannot have projects that are dragging and dragging and dragging. We can't keep ending in a place where this is the end of a sprint or the end of a cycle and we still can't see the end of it, or we have to make so many cuts and compromises at the last minute that it's not the quality of... or it's not really matching what it was supposed to be in the first place. When those problems are happening or... Also by the way, this is surfacing at the exact level. (01:10:22): Imagine, you're the CPO, you're the CTO, and you are supposed to be answering to, "How's that work going?" (01:10:30): And it's like, "Well, actually, we're working on it. I can just think of a couple of times when I needed to go to Jason, and he expected me to be making progress on something and I had gotten nowhere on it. And that feeling when you are with top leadership in the room and you don't have a good answer for where you are on something is like... Oh, it's brutal, right? And then from the CEO's perspective, it's like, "Where's the movement? We're running a business here. Really, nothing is shipping still?" (01:11:03): This can't just keep happening. So there's some recognition somewhere either at the higher levels or within the team of, we don't want to keep dragging, we don't want to keep being lost in the weeds, and then this can be the activation energy. You gather the power to be like, "Okay, we actually want to try something different." (01:11:26): And in that case, what I would say is what usually works best is, okay, we're going to try a pilot project, and what we want to do is, as you said, choose a problem that's important enough to all of us that we think it's meaningful, it's going to be worth trying to do well. And it doesn't have to be six weeks. It could be something that is a little bit smaller, maybe you feel comfortable taking on three week thing for the first time. What's important is just matching these things together. (01:11:55): Here's a problem that we actually care about. It's timely, something that we would like to be shipped soon. It's not so small that we're not going to actually learn this new muscle, and it's big enough that it's going to feel like we really achieved something. So maybe that's going to be four weeks, maybe it's going to be six, maybe it's three, I don't know. And then getting to a place where we wrestle a bit with the problem to get the problem narrowed down. We get into our shaping session, and then we do our best. Do you know what I mean? And usually, what happens too is if we have an engineering team that's going to become free to do this work for those X number of weeks, that's the upper limit on how long we can spend to shape, and that's another real life thing, is sometimes we talk about if... (01:12:51): On the one hand there's this universe of never ending documents back and forth to get feedback and comments, and then on the other hand there's like the team is going to be available. We're trying to actually do this, so actually, we've got a week to shape because engineering needs to kick off next week. Do you know what I mean? That's a little bit more the real scenario when you're actually in this aligned world of we want to ship something now.
turns.zh:
不会，我不会那么做。我认为关键在于，当你能让产品和工程团队坐到一起开规划会时，就说明你已经取得了很大进展。能做到这一步就已经很棒了。  
哦，真正困难的地方在于，要让产品和工程团队达成一致意见。我们不能让项目拖拖拉拉、一拖再拖。不能在冲刺结束或周期结束时，发现问题仍未解决，最后只能仓促修改和妥协，这样既影响了质量，也背离了最初的设想。当这些问题出现时……顺便说一句，这种情况正是在最高层级显现的。（01:10:22）：想象一下，你是首席产品官或首席技术官，被问到“进展如何？”  
（01:10:30）：你可能会说：“嗯，我们正在努力解决。但有几次我需要向杰森汇报进展时，他却期望我已经取得了实质性进展，而我却毫无进展。当你面对高层领导时，却无法给出一个合理的解释，这种感觉简直太糟糕了。” 
（01:11:03）：这种情况不能再继续下去了。所以，无论是高层还是团队内部，都意识到不能再拖延，不能再陷入无休止的纠缠，这就是启动变革的能量源泉。你要鼓起勇气，说：“好吧，我们真的要尝试一些不同的方法。” 
（01:11:26）：在这种情况下，我认为最有效的做法是启动试点项目。正如你所说，选择一个对我们所有人都重要的问题——我们认为这个问题有意义，值得努力做好。试点不必持续六周，可以稍微小一点，比如先尝试三周。关键是把这些因素协调起来。 
（01:11:55）：这是一个我们真正关心的难题。它时机恰当，是我们希望尽快上线的产品。问题规模不至于小到无法学习新技能，也足够大，让我们能切实感受到有所收获。可能需要四周，也许六周，或者三周，我不知道。然后我们会花些时间深入研究问题，缩小问题的范围。进入规划阶段后，我们会全力以赴。你懂我的意思吧？通常，如果工程团队在接下来的几周内可以专注于这项工作，试点项目的持续时间就以此为上限。这是现实情况——有时我们会纠结于无休止的文档反馈和修改，而团队又需要腾出时间参与项目。实际上，因为工程团队下周就要开始工作了，所以我们只有一周的时间进行规划。你懂我的意思吧？当你真正身处这种希望上线产品的协作环境中时，情况会更清晰明了。
now.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, real life constraints. That's a really helpful way of telling you how much time you have to do this. For people that are just like, "I don't know, any friends that are using this. It's like weird, this way of working. It's not a thing I hear about all the time." What can you say to them to help them be like, "Okay, I should actually give this a try. Here's how many people are using it. Here's impact that you've seen." Anything you can share that would help them get over that hump?
turns.zh: 是啊，这就是现实生活中的种种限制。这真是个很有效的方法，能让你清楚自己还有多少时间去做这件事。对于那些只会说“我不知道，有没有朋友在用这个。这种工作方式太奇怪了，我可没经常听说这种情况”的人，你该怎么跟他们说才能让他们愿意尝试呢？比如，“看看有多少人在用这个，再讲讲你亲眼见证的成效。”有没有什么实例能帮助他们克服这种心理障碍？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: I would say wait until it hurts more. If the unfamiliarity is the big problem with it, then maybe the things are fine. Because it's not like this is the only way. It's more like, changing is really hard, and if there's a good reason to do it and it's like, look, we've done it the old way. We've tried different experiments. We've even already churned through a new head of product, or we've got a different CTO in and we're still having the same problems, then there comes a point where it's like, I know that this is uncomfortable, and I don't know somebody who's done it, but I think we need to try something different because we can't continue this way.
turns.zh: 我觉得得等到痛苦感加剧了才行。要是大家觉得陌生感是主要问题，那或许其他方面还不错。因为这又不是唯一的解决方案。关键在于，改变实在太难了。如果有充分的理由去做这件事——比如，我们已经按照老方法试过了，也做过各种尝试，甚至换了产品负责人，或者换了首席技术官，但问题依然存在——那时候就该反思了：我知道这很不舒服，我身边也没人成功过，但我觉得我们必须尝试新方法，不能再这么下去了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a great answer. Following that same thread, just what are signs that it's time to try something? What sort of pain do you often see that's like, okay, you shouldn't look into this seriously?
turns.zh: 这回答真棒。顺着这个思路，再问问，什么时候该尝试新方法了？你通常会看到哪些迹象，能让你觉得应该认真考虑一下了？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: There are pains all along the journey. So I think the place where it's most obvious is at the end of the line when we thought we were going to be done and this thing is just dragging and dragging and dragging. The teams, we're not shipping things. We're running in place. We keep going in circles on this like we don't see the end. Of course, that's the culmination, but there's also a lot of pain points along the way. (01:15:11): So if we go all the way upstream, if we go to the source of a project, sales talk to a customer... You know what I mean? Or sales talk to a lead, and they have this idea of this thing we need to build, or the CEO had this idea in the shower the other day, or the product team did a whole bunch of research and they have a big case for why this is the thing that's important to build next. Whatever it is, there's a source from the business perspective of this is the thing we should do next. (01:15:44): If we just say dashboard and we don't negotiate what that means, if we just say calendar and we don't negotiate what that actually is, then what do we experience? This fuzzy thing where it's really hard to get to a conclusive answer about, yeah, that's what we need to go do. It's like the ever expanding blob. So if you've felt that before, that's already a first pain. And then of course, where does it go from there? So we say calendar, so we don't know what it means, but we say calendar, so now we give it to product and we've either got a whole bunch of Figma files or we have the PRD with a million requirements about what a great calendar is. Of course, I don't want to be cruel to the people who are putting their hearts into that work, because the Figma file is beautiful. It's just coming a little early. And the PRD is full of a lot of true things that are probably really important for decision-making in the project, but the way that it's packaged at that moment isn't something that gets absorbed. You write this document and I'm sorry, who actually reads it? You know what I mean? I know it's painful, but it's like that. And then even when we try to read it, because it wasn't shaped and we didn't get down to it's this, it's that, it's that, and that's how it works, it's hard to walk away from reading that and have anything that's in your head as, this is what we're going to go build. It's like a million puzzle pieces that you're going to have to solve. So what we see is either there's the Figma file and then there's the pushback from engineers. There's the PRD, but then it's like, okay, but we still don't actually know what to build. (01:17:40): There's all those things where, instead of moving forward, there's more and more questions, more and more pushback, more and more going back to the drawing board. So that's another big indicator that something is going wrong. And then when we're in the building and we thought we knew what we agreed to, we thought we all said, "Yeah, this is what we want to go make," and it's just more and more questions coming out. More and more unexpected complexity, things that we didn't anticipate, and it just doesn't feel like we're getting warmer and coming closer. It just feels like it's getting harder and harder. Those are all the signs that whatever process you use, that there's a lack of clear shaping and there's a lack of clear framing because there's a lack of clarity around what it is that we're doing.
turns.zh: 整个过程充满了痛苦。最明显的痛点出现在项目尾声——当我们以为终于可以收工时，却发现进展迟迟未能推进。团队成员只是在原地踏步，不断重复循环，却始终看不到终点。当然，终点是关键节点，但整个过程也布满了无数的阻碍。（01:15:11）：如果我们追溯到项目源头——比如销售与客户沟通需求，CEO在淋浴时灵光一现，或者产品团队经过大量调研后提出的某个构想——无论最初的灵感源自何处，最终都需要明确项目的目标。（01:15:44）：如果我们只提“仪表盘”却不明确其含义，提“日历”却不定义其具体功能，最终会陷入混乱的境地。（01:17:40）：当产品团队提交精美的Figma文件或堆满要求的PRD时，开发人员却无法理解其核心诉求。这些文档看似完美，却因缺乏清晰的框架而难以落地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we started recording, you made this interesting point that there's always talk of feature factories and that rarely are they actually efficient factories. They don't actually work. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 在我们开始录制之前，你提到了一个很有趣的观点：人们常提及“功能工厂”，但现实中这类工厂很少真正高效运作。它们根本行不通。能否详细谈谈这个问题？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. Well, I understand what the feature factory critique is supposed to be. It's actually to the framing point of we're not negotiating the value and the outcome we're trying to get from something. We're just taking it and building it. And then of course, in the end, according to the feature factory critique, we just built it because somebody said we should build it, and then people didn't use it and didn't value it, and the product is just getting bloated. The thing is that, I would say if you have a feature factory, meaning you're continually cranking out features, you're probably quite healthy. All you need to do is feed a different input to the beginning of the factory. (01:19:18): What most teams are struggling with is that they don't have predictable repeatable shipping of things. At least from my experience, the bigger really widespread struggle is, stuff isn't moving, it's dragging. I can't see the end. I'm losing my... I'm feeling burned out. You know what I mean? It's not exciting to work on this anymore, all that a thing.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，我理解“功能工厂”批评的核心在于，我们并没有真正协商功能的价值和预期效果，只是直接着手开发。最终按照批评者的说法，我们之所以开发某个功能，只是因为有人要求我们做，而用户并不使用它，也不认可其价值，导致产品变得臃肿。但我要说，如果你真有功能工厂机制——也就是持续产出功能——那说明你的团队运作得相当健康。只需要给工厂入口处输入不同的需求即可。（01:19:18）：多数团队面临的难题是无法实现可预测、可重复的交付。至少以我的经验来看，更普遍的挑战是进展缓慢，停滞不前。我看不到尽头，精疲力竭，心灰意冷。你们懂我的意思吧？再做下去就毫无热情了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe last question here is what's the sweet spot stage for a company to start using Shape Up? You basically worked in this way from the very beginning when it was just three people. What do you find... Should startups that are just starting out start working in this way, or do you find it's more useful later on?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题：公司何时应该开始使用 Shape Up？你们从三人团队起步就采用了这种模式。你们认为……初创公司是否应该从一开始就采用这种方式，还是说后期效果更好？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: We didn't formalize it until we had to, and there was a long time where there wasn't a fixed length for projects. There was just an understanding of the urgency and a feeling of what too long felt like. And it didn't actually click into, oh, this is a cycle length and this is six weeks, and then we pause, and this is who comes together to make the decision of what's the next project, and here's who is mainly doing the shape. You know what I mean? All that stuff didn't get solved until we had reached a certain size. Usually, the main tipping point if we start from smaller to big is there's a phase when the founders are still involved in everything, and so it doesn't matter what your process is, it's going to be fine. (01:20:40): But then you start to hire the first other people and then for the first time you try to delegate some of those things and the founders try to be less involved, and that's often where a lot of these problems start to appear. And the founders start to ask themselves like, "We used to be fast, and now we hired people because we needed to scale, but now we're slow. So how do we be fast again? Because we know what-
turns.zh: 我们直到必要时才正式化流程。很长一段时间里，项目没有固定时长。大家只是凭直觉判断时间是否过长。没有明确的周期时长标准，也没有六周的固定周期。然后停下来，由团队共同决定下一个项目，由谁来主导规划。直到公司规模达到一定程度，这些才逐步规范化。通常，从小型到大型的转变关键点在于创始人是否还深度参与所有环节。无论流程如何，初期都运转良好。（01:20:40）但当开始招聘员工，试图将某些职责下放，创始人又试图减少参与度时，问题就接踵而至。创始人会反思：“我们曾经行动迅速，现在为了扩张招了人，但速度却变慢了。如何重拾敏捷性？毕竟我们深知——”

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: ... well. So like, "How will we be fast again?" Because we know what it's like. If we just got back in there as founders and got our hands dirty, like we could make this go. But how do I get the people that we've brought in to make these trade-offs and make these decisions and how do I get the work to flow again? So that's something that we definitely see there. So that's a really good moment. I'm onboarding new people. I don't know what to tell them how to work. I don't want to introduce a bunch of scrum rituals. Just winging it on Kanban isn't working, because they don't have enough clarity around what to go after. So I have to babysit them all the time. You know what I mean? Like these kinds of things. (01:21:40): There is another extreme, which is I... We've already gone past that. We've been scrum or whatever for years. The company has been growing, like revenue is coming in, like sales is doing their job, like things are running. But man, nothing is getting out the door. And we're years in and we have an entrenched development. We have like an entrenched engineering team, which is a wall away from an entrenched product team and everybody's apart. And this thing is like, we're like stuck. (01:22:19): And that is more where there's going to be some tensions that are starting to appear at the executive level. There's going to be some finger pointing. There's going to be some like, "Why isn't this moving? Why isn't this happening? How can we be spending so much money in all these engineers and we don't have anything to show for it?" And that's a point where there can be kind of a... Some hard conversations need to start happening about, "How do we actually start to negotiate around how we spend time?" And we can't just have endless refactorings and infrastructure projects, but we need to be actually building things that we can sell again.
turns.zh:
嗯。所以就像，“我们要怎样才能再次提速？”因为我们深有体会。如果我们能重返创始人角色，亲力亲为，或许就能推动业务发展。但我该如何让新加入的团队成员做出权衡和决策，又该如何让工作重回正轨？这确实是我们面临的难题。所以这确实是个关键时刻。我正在招募新员工，却不知道该如何指导他们的工作流程。我不想引入一堆Scrum仪式，但只靠Kanban这种临时应付的办法也不行，因为他们对工作重点缺乏清晰的认知。所以我不得不时刻手把手指导他们。懂我的意思吧？就是这种情况。

（01:21:40）：还有另一种极端情况，我们已经度过了那个阶段。我们多年来一直采用Scrum之类的框架。公司一直在增长，营收不断攀升，销售团队各司其职，一切运转正常。但天啊，没有任何成果产出。经过多年发展，工程团队已经根深蒂固，产品团队也各自为政，彼此隔阂重重。这时候我们就陷入了僵局。

（01:22:19）：这种情况下，高管层往往会出现一些摩擦。比如互相指责：“为什么进展如此缓慢？为什么一事无成？我们花了那么多钱养活这些工程师，却没有任何成果可展示？”这个时候就需要坐下来认真讨论：“我们该如何合理分配时间？”不能永远沉溺于无休止的重构和基础设施项目，而是要真正开发出能带来收益的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an idea.
turns.zh: 真是个好主意。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. You know? But it can... There are a lot of engineering orgs that have been standing around for a while and it's all refactoring all day and tech debt and stuff like that. And there's reasons why all those things got there, but there comes a point where we have to figure out how to cut through it and make some hard choices so that we can carve out time to build the stuff that's actually going to be needle moving again and not just sustaining us where we are to run in place.
turns.zh: 是啊。你懂吧？但这种情况……有很多工程团队停滞不前，每天都在重构代码、处理技术债务之类的问题。这些问题的根源固然有其客观原因，但到了某个阶段，我们就必须割舍掉这些累赘，果断做出取舍，这样才能腾出时间开发真正能推动业务发展的产品，而不仅仅是维持现状。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine this latter bucket is who you mostly work with, the kind of companies that bring you in.
turns.zh: 我猜后者才是你主要接触的客户类型，也就是那些请你加入的公司。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: It's been a lot of the folks who still remember what it was like to be fast and they're kind of newly too big and they don't like being slow. I've had a lot of that. I think that your intuition is right. That the market for the last category is the biggest, but it's hard to reach them. It's not easy to talk about these things. These are sensitive topics. Do you know what I mean? Like, "Our engineering team isn't shipping," and it's happening at leadership level. There's a ton of complaints happening deeper in the org, but nobody down in the org can change anything. At the end of the day, it's actually the interface at the executive level of being able to say, "How are we using our time? We have to change something."
turns.zh: 这类客户大多还记得快速迭代的快感，但如今规模太大，又不甘心拖慢脚步。我接触过不少这类客户。我觉得你的直觉是对的。最后一类客户的市场规模最大，但很难触达。他们对这些话题很敏感，你懂我的意思吧？比如“我们的工程团队交付不了成果”，这种抱怨在高管层级已经屡见不鲜，但组织内部却无人能改变现状。归根结底，关键在于高管层能否勇于发声：“我们该如何合理分配时间？我们必须做出改变。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make it even more concrete in that first bucket, what's the size of org that you find is most in need of this? It's like, "How many engineers?" Or is it like when they hire the first PM? Like what's kind of the-
turns.zh: 更具体地说，在第一个阶段，你认为最需要这种帮助的组织规模是多大？比如，“需要多少工程师？”或者是在他们聘请首位产品经理时的情况？比如具体是怎样的——

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: I sometimes have the like, "How the heck do I hire the first PM and what do they do?" conversation. But usually, it's later than that. It's after they hired the first PM, after they hired the second PM, and maybe even the third. And they're getting to the... Product and engineering together are like 30, 50 people and it's like, "We thought we put everybody in the right roles. We kind of did what we were supposed to do and everything is just grinding. And why are we so slow?
turns.zh: 我有时会进行类似的对话，比如“我到底该怎么招聘首位产品经理？他们的职责是什么？”。但通常情况下，这类讨论往往发生得更晚。比如在聘请了首位产品经理、第二位产品经理，甚至第三位产品经理之后，当产品和工程团队规模达到30到50人左右时，他们会发现：“我们以为每个人都找到了合适的岗位，按部就班地推进工作，但进展依然缓慢。为什么会这样？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect. So 30 to 50-ish people seems like a good time to... Basically, you're finding that's when things start to really break down.
turns.zh: 太好了。所以30到50人左右似乎是一个关键节点。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: That's when they show themselves and I think... I mean, if someone hears this and it all starts to make sense and they're earlier in that wave, then of course the earlier that you can anticipate it, the better, right?
turns.zh: 这正是问题暴露的时刻。我觉得……如果有人听了这些内容后豁然开朗，并且他们正处于这个阶段的早期，那么越早预见到这些问题，效果就越好，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That's a good point.
turns.zh: 没错。这是个很好的观点。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: So if you're-
turns.zh: 所以如果你——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When it's too late is when they come out so-
turns.zh: 等到问题出现时才意识到，那就太晚了。这就是为什么他们会寻求帮助——

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: I mainly hear about it when it's too late. That's why they're reaching out-
turns.zh: 我听到的大多都是在问题已经发生后才开始求助。这就是为什么他们会主动联系——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So maybe closer to 30. Okay.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以可能在30人左右。好的。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Honestly, I think it starts the first project where, for example, the founding engineer is hands off and then the new hire is taking over responsibility. Or the person who was like sort of founder/CEO is first giving it to a PM to kind of thinking they're going to carry it through. And then, it's not exactly meeting their expectations of what they thought was going to happen. I think that's when those disconnects actually start. It's the first step away from the work where the seeds of all of these problems actually start.
turns.zh: 说实话，我认为问题始于第一个项目。比如，创始工程师逐渐放权，新人接手责任。或者原本担任创始人/CEO角色的人将职责交给产品经理，期望对方能继续推进工作。但结果往往与预期相差甚远。我认为正是从这时起，各种问题的种子开始萌芽，偏离正轨的第一步由此产生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about Basecamp and how maybe not every company can operate like Basecamp. Before we get there, is there anything else along the lines of Shape Up that you want to add or share?
turns.zh: 我想谈谈Basecamp，以及并非所有公司都能像Basecamp那样运营。在深入探讨之前，你是否还有关于Shape Up之类的其他见解或经验可以分享？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. There's one key thing, which is the role of the PM. I think what we see today, out of necessity in a lot of teams, is that the PMs spend a lot of time chasing around inside of the build phase, inside the time box, to try and make sure that people aren't stuck and getting lost in the weeds and try and keep things moving. And it can sometimes be too close to project management rather than product management. (01:26:43): And what we see in Shape Up teams when they hit their stride is that the PM moves upstream. So the PM is less busy with, "How do I get this project to not be in a bad state when it's getting built?" And they're way more in, "How do I understand the business context? How do I narrow down the problem? How do I negotiate back and forth with maybe the CPO who brought this to me to understand where the core of it is?" That really getting the deeper understanding of the business and the problem and the customer domain and like what problem is worth solving and what's even slice of that problem is the valuable slice to argue that we should spend a few weeks on. That's the place where the PMs can really contribute a lot in the Shape Up world. That's kind of what they do, rather than shepherding the process or being a ritual master or something like that.
turns.zh: 是的。有一点很关键，那就是产品经理（PM）的角色。我认为如今在很多团队中，出于无奈，PM们往往在构建阶段、时间框架内花费大量时间四处奔波，试图确保团队成员不会陷入困境、迷失方向，并推动项目进展。但有时这种做法更偏向于项目管理而非产品管理。（01:26:43）而在 Shape Up 团队中，当他们步入正轨后，PM 会向上游转移。也就是说，PM 不再纠结于“如何避免项目在构建阶段陷入糟糕状态”，而是更多地专注于“如何理解业务背景？如何界定问题核心？如何与提出需求的首席产品官（CPO）反复沟通以明确核心诉求？”这种深层理解业务、问题及客户领域的能力，以及如何判断某个问题是否值得解决、某个问题切片是否值得深入探讨的能力，才是在 Shape Up 世界中 PM 真正能创造巨大价值的地方。这才是他们的核心职责，而非简单地监管流程或充当仪式大师之类角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds pretty wonderful. I've been doing some thinking about what an AI-oriented world does to the role of PM and it feels like very similar to that actually, where the building now is going to happen for you with AI tooling. And that means the bigger question now is like, "What the hell should I build? And is the thing I've built right and correct and likely to work?" And it feels like this is similar, it's like the PM spending a lot more time upfront thinking through what to build. And then, the building is a lot more hands off. So hands off it gets done in like five minutes when you're just like, "Well, build this thing for me." "There it is."
turns.zh: 这听起来确实很棒。我一直在思考人工智能导向的世界对 PM 角色的影响，发现其实非常相似——现在构建工作将由人工智能工具代劳。这意味着更大的挑战在于，“我到底该构建什么？我构建的东西是否正确、有效且易于落地？”这与 PM 需要提前深入思考构建内容十分相似，而后续的构建工作则变得更加被动。当你只需说“帮我把这个东西建起来”时，五分钟就能搞定。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. Let's see. Let's see. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。让我想想。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's see.
turns.zh: 让我想想。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: I'm also very curious. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我也很好奇。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. What a wild time. Okay. Let's talk about Basecamp. I think we talked about this ahead of the podcast that... You want people to know that Basecamp is very unique and not everyone can work the way Basecamp works. Just talk about your insight there and your advice there when people see all this advice coming out of Basecamp.
turns.zh: 天哪。真是疯狂的时代。好吧，让我们谈谈 Basecamp。我记得在播客前我们讨论过……你想让人们知道 Basecamp 非常独特，并非所有团队都能照搬其模式。能否谈谈你的见解，以及当人们看到 Basecamp 推出的各种建议时，你会给出怎样的建议？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: I got to tell you, I had no idea how unique we were until I was outside and there are so many things. For example, it's a lot of the things that people ask me about that are not in the book that started to reveal those things to me. That's so many things that I was just taking for granted. I mean, every designer codes. (01:29:05): Imagine, if every designer codes and I don't just mean HTML. I mean, like running the app locally, going in to the place where that view is rendered to make that thing look the way that they want it to look or whatever, right? I mean, like really codes, every designer. So every designer codes, where's the wall between design and engineering? Where is the moment where you arrive with the Figma file and then the disappointment and all of your hopes get destroyed because the engineer is telling you no, right? Like those moments don't even exist in that world. (01:29:42): And then, also, I think also there was this lack of distance between sort of the business objective, the thing that we're trying to... The reason we want to maybe do this project and the blessing of the founders and the... Like, there wasn't this kind of executives far away with some big targets and then some layer of PM and then some building. I mean, the founders were always there, right there in the problem definition still. (01:30:14): I mean, I can't say today, but I mean up until 2021 when I was still there. So it meant that there was so much clarity all the time around what we're solving and why and why we're making time for it. And then, of course, on the engineering side as well. I mean, imagine, you have no sales org, you have no marketing. That all of selling and marketing is happening by the unicorn founders. So it means that there isn't contention for engineering time, that there isn't like all these different sources of requests that you have to wrestle with, (01:30:50): And David did such an extraordinary job of... I mean, the more I see the real world, the more I'm amazed at how every six weeks, there was clear runway in engineering of like, "We have time for whatever the... Whatever we'd agreed together is the most important thing." Just blank check like six weeks at a time. Not a blank check, but you know what I mean? Like a blank six weeks, yeah?
turns.zh:
不得不说，在走出办公室之前，我从未意识到我们有多与众不同。周围有太多东西需要去处理。比如，人们问我很多书中未提及的内容，这些问题才让我逐渐意识到自己的认知局限。原来有太多事情我曾想当然地认为理所当然。比如，每个设计师都会写代码（01:29:05）——我说的可不是HTML基础知识，而是诸如本地调试应用、调整视图呈现效果、优化交互体验之类的高级操作。每个设计师都在深度参与代码开发，这就模糊了设计与工程之间的界限。当你带着Figma文件找工程师，却被告知“不行”时，那种失望感和希望破灭的瞬间根本不存在于那个世界。

（01:29:42）此外，商业目标与工程团队之间的沟通也更加顺畅。创始人始终深度参与项目定义，没有遥不可及的宏伟目标，也没有层层叠叠的项目经理和开发团队。创始人始终身处问题解决的第一线。

（01:30:14）至少在2021年我离开前是这样的。这意味着我们始终能清晰地把握解决问题的核心、目标所在，以及为此投入时间的合理性。工程团队方面同样如此——没有销售团队，没有市场部门，所有销售和营销工作都由独角兽创始人亲自操刀。这意味着工程资源不会被其他需求分割，团队能专注于核心任务。

（01:30:50）大卫做得非常出色。越是深入现实世界，我就越惊叹于每六周一次的清晰路线规划：“我们有充足时间完成共识目标。”这就像一次六周的空白支票。倒不是字面意义上的空白支票，而是六周无干扰的专注时间。明白我的意思吧？六周纯粹的专注时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Again and again and again, years without end. Keeping that engineering capacity focused on readiness for product and totally leaning into what's exciting to do to build for the product. And not getting lost in all this refactoring and new infrastructure and technical debt and stuff like that. I mean, those are amazing. So those are some really big differences. And it doesn't mean that you have to be Basecamp to do Shape Up. But what it does mean is that when we say, "Oh, just have a shaping session and if you have the pressure of the time box, then you can make trade-offs together." It's like, "Well, if we are used to having a big wall between, for example, engineering and design, then we're going to have to learn..." Somebody who wants to start shaping is going to have to learn like, "Well, oh, I need to figure out who to bring together and how to have that session and how do we interact with each other. So that we are combining all of that knowledge that maybe at Basecamp was all in the same head in a lot of cases."
turns.zh: 年复一年，不停重复。保持工程团队专注于产品准备，全心投入激动人心的产品建设，而非深陷重构、新基础设施、技术债务等杂务之中。这些工作固然重要，但差距显著。这并不意味着你非得像Basecamp那样才能实现Shape Up。但这意味着，当我们提议“开个塑形会议吧”，如果受限于时间框架，就可以共同权衡取舍。这就好比说：“嗯，如果我们习惯于在工程与设计之间设置高墙，那就得学会如何打破隔阂。”想要开展塑形会议的人必须学会：如何组织团队、如何设计流程、如何有效协作。这样才能整合那些在Basecamp可能由一个人统筹的知识。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such an important point for people to hear, because there's so many people that come on podcasts like this and share, "Here's how to do it," based on their experience. And there's so many just assumptions about their resources, the people they hire, the way the founders operate. Like no sales team, I think that's like... I don't even think about that.
turns.zh: 这对人们来说是个非常重要的观点，因为有太多人来听这类播客时，会根据自己的经验分享"应该这样做"。但他们对资源、聘请的团队、创始人的运营方式往往存在诸多想当然。比如没有销售团队？我觉得这简直……我甚至都不会考虑这种情况。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. Imagine, no such thing as a request from sales, yeah? No such thing as pressure of like, "We need this thing in order to upsell or to close this deal." Never.
turns.zh: 是啊。你想象一下，如果没有销售部门的需求，那会怎样？没有那种"为了追加销售或达成交易，我们必须这么做"的压力？从来没有过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds like you're in this Basecamp... By the way, was it called 37signals? Like it's interesting you call it Basecamp not 37signal.
turns.zh: 听起来你之前在 Basecamp 工作……顺便问一下，它之前叫 37signals 吗？有趣的是，你现在称它为 Basecamp，而不是 37signals。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, so it's just like the timing of when I left. We were originally 37signals and then Basecamp became so big that we renamed ourselves to Basecamp.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，我离开的时机正好。我们最初叫 37signals，但后来 Basecamp 发展得太大了，所以我们改名为 Basecamp。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't know that.
turns.zh: 我不知道这个情况。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. And then, so for example, on the book, it says Shape Up and there's a Basecamp logo on the bottom, not a 37signals logo. But then, since I went back, so it's 37signals again. So I sometimes struggle with I don't know what to call it but it's both. Whatever people can recognize, it's the same powerhouse.
turns.zh: 是的。比如说，在书里提到 Shape Up，底部有 Basecamp 的标志，而不是 37signals 的标志。但后来我回去工作后，又改回了 37signals。所以有时我也不知道该怎么称呼它，但反正都是同一家公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Cool. I'm glad I'm not the only one that's confused. But 37signal is the current name. Great.
turns.zh: 好的。太好了。很高兴我不是唯一一个感到困惑的人。但 37signals 是现在的名称。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you said that it felt like you left and it was like this bubble you got out of. Was there like a moment where you're like, "You wrote this book. Everyone..." You're like, "Hey, this is how you should work," and then you're like, "Oh, wait. This doesn't actually work in real life for a lot of people."? Is there a moment there?
turns.zh: 你说离开后，感觉就像走出了一个泡沫。有没有那么一个时刻，你意识到"你写了这本书，但现实中很多人做不到"？有没有这样的时刻？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: It wasn't that this doesn't work, I was just in a foreign country. It was like we tried it and it didn't work. One of the common things I would hear is the projects kept running over. "We weren't finishing them at the end of the cycle. They kept running over and running over." And then, I would be like, "Huh. So can you show me your shaping work?" And then, they would show me a PRD and I'd be like, "That doesn't look like what's in the book." And again like, "Can you show me your shaping work?" And they'd show me like a bunch of Figma files. (01:34:21): And then, what I started to understand was like we have some people in a role who were used to making a certain artifact at a certain step and they just kept doing that. And I didn't appreciate... It took me a while to realize like, "There's no engineer in the picture here." And it was when we started to actually do the course, I said... Well, I did actually a couple projects where I helped teams hands-on and I learned that they... (01:34:50): It was the first actually consulting project that I did where I helped a team who was stuck. And what we did was we chose the engineer who was best suited to come over to product and be there in the shaping. And that was the moment when it was like, "Ah. Now, I'm in the world I know again," when we had all of that mixed in the same room again. And so, that was kind of like... That was really something... I mean, it was a total learning curve for me and there's a lot of things like that. But that was, for example, a really big one. It's like, "Oh, we have to get engineering in there."
turns.zh: 不是说这方法不行，而是我当时在国外。就像我们尝试过但没成功一样。我常听到的一个常见问题是项目总是超期。"我们总是在周期结束时还没完成它们，不断拖延。"然后我会问："嗯，那能让我看看你们的成型工作吗？"他们就会给我看一份PRD文件，我会说："这看起来和书里写的不一样。"接着我又问："能让我看看你们的成型工作吗？"他们就给我看一堆Figma文件。（01:34:21）后来我逐渐意识到，有些人习惯在某个阶段制作特定的工件，然后一直重复这个流程。我没有意识到……过了一段时间我才意识到，"这里根本没有工程师参与。" 直到我们真正开始做课程时，我才意识到……嗯，我确实参与过几个项目，亲自帮助团队解决问题，我发现他们……（01:34:50）这是我做的第一个真正的咨询项目，帮助一个陷入困境的团队。我们选择了最适合参与产品成型工作的工程师。就在那一刻，我感觉"啊，现在我又回到了熟悉的领域"，因为所有相关人员又聚集在同一间会议室里了。所以，这真的……这真的意义非凡。我的意思是，这对我来说完全是能力提升的过程，还有很多类似的经历。但这确实是其中最重要的一次。就像，"哦，我们必须让工程团队参与进来"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're the type of guest I most love having on this podcast, because you basically work with many, many companies, study what's working, what's not. You're not in the clouds pontificating about something. You're working with teams to make things better. And then, you take all of that learning, put it into a book, and share with us all. And so, the ROI is just incredible for us all because you've spent so much time doing this and you've actually done the work. You're not just in theory about it. So this is amazing. But we're not done yet. One question I wanted to ask is, Jason was tweeting that there's... He's working on a follow-up Shape Up book. What's happening there? Are you involved in that? What's the story?
turns.zh: 你是我最喜欢邀请到这个播客的嘉宾，因为你基本上和很多公司合作过，研究什么方法有效，什么方法无效。你不是高高在上地空谈理论，而是与团队合作让事情变得更好。然后，你把所有这些经验总结成书，与我们分享。对我们所有人来说，投资回报率简直难以置信，因为你投入了大量时间去做这些事，而且确实付出了实际行动。不是空谈理论。所以这太棒了。但我们还没结束。我想问一个问题，杰森在推特上提到正在写一本后续的《Shape Up》书。进展如何？你参与其中了吗？情况如何？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: So I also saw the tweet. And I have to admit, I was a little surprised when I saw this tweet, but I had had a conversation with Jason a year earlier. And he reached out and he said, "Hey, we're thinking about doing a second edition of the book." And my first reaction... Imagine, I was actually really in the middle of learning all these things that teams need to learn in order to catch up to what was natural for Basecamp to do. And so, for me, it was like, "Interesting. I have a lot of new things. I have a lot of new ideas. Maybe collaborating on the second edition could make sense." (01:36:46): But what I understood was that what he wanted to do was to make an updated version of how they work, because that's always been a big thing of how... I should use the right name, 37signals, of how they market and also how they lead is they like to really show a clear example. Not like, "This is how you could do it. This is how some people do it," but like, "This is how we do it." (01:37:09): And I think it's their strength that they are very, very clear like, "This is how we do it and take it or leave it." What I understood was that if I did another version of the book that was just how Basecamp does it, I think it would leave so much opportunity on the table. Like there's so many people where what they need to learn is more like, "How can it come closer to where I am? If I have the wall today between product and engineering, how do I bring the right people together into a shaping session? How do we actually do that? How do I overcome all of these little challenges because this is so far from our current way of working?" (01:37:44): So the work that I'm doing with, for example, with shaping in real life is all about those gaps. And then, I don't know what's going to be in the second edition because they are... I guess someone there is going to be working on that. But what I'm guessing is it's going to be an update on kind of, "Up on top of the mountain over here, this is what Basecamp is doing." So hopefully, it'll be a cool thing to look at as like, "Here's a model of what they're doing." And then the question is, "What can I take from that and what do I need in order to actually be able to make it work in the real situation I'm in?" And that's kind of where... Well, that's my focus.
turns.zh: 是的，我也看到了那条推文。不得不承认，看到这条推文时我有点惊讶，但一年前我和杰森有过一次谈话。他当时联系我说道："嘿，我们正在考虑推出这本书的第二版。"我的第一反应是……想象一下，我当时正全心投入学习团队需要掌握的那些知识，以便赶上Basecamp的先进做法。对我来说，这感觉很奇妙。我有很多新想法、新思路，可能合作完成第二版会是个不错的主意。（01:36:46）但我理解的是，他们想做的是更新版本，展示他们的工作方式，因为这始终是他们的一大特色——他们喜欢通过清晰的示例来展示如何做事，而不是说"你可以这样做"，或者"有些人是这样做的"，而是"我们就是这样做的，要么接受，要么离开"。（01:37:09）我认为他们的优势在于，他们非常明确地传达"我们就是这样做的，要么接受，要么离开"。如果我只是照搬Basecamp的做法来写新版书籍，那会错失很多机会。比如，有很多人需要学习的不是"如何让它更贴近我的现状"，而是"如果我现在面临产品和工程之间的隔阂，该如何把合适的人召集到塑形会议上？该如何具体操作？该如何克服这些小挑战？因为这和我们现有的工作方式相差太远了"。（01:37:44）所以我现在所做的工作，比如在现实生活中推动塑形，就是针对这些差距的。至于第二版的内容，我不太清楚，因为应该有人在负责编写。但我猜它会更新现状，展示"我们现在在山顶上是这样做的"。希望它能成为一个很好的参考，让人们能借鉴其中的模式，并思考"我能从中学到什么，又需要什么才能真正在自己的实际环境中应用这些方法？"这才是关键所在……嗯，这就是我的关注点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting. Thank you for sharing. It sounds like a fork. You forked it and these are going potentially in different directions but inspired by each other.
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。谢谢你分享。听起来这像是一次分叉。你分叉了项目，虽然可能朝着不同的方向发展，但彼此相互启发。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Totally.
turns.zh: 嗯，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. Ryan, is there anything else that you want to share before we wrap up?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。瑞安，在我们结束之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: One thing I could throw out there is sometimes people reach out to me because their projects aren't shipping, there's a lot of struggle, there's a lot of lack of clarity. But the root cause is actually that the input at the very beginning of the process is too unclear or... Like we don't actually know what's important to customers or we're not actually sure where the value is or this kind of a thing. So there is this link, this framing step that we talked about of, "What is really the problem?", before we go into shaping. (01:39:11): This is the link to product strategy also. And this is the place where it can be really useful to reach for a lot of, for example, Bob Moesta stuff with the Jobs-to-be-Done and the demand-side work, trying to get clear about big... So that's the tool that I reach for at that phase. And you can think of kind of this... Before the problem definition, there's this question of like, "What's the demand? Where are people struggling? Where is really the place, the itch they're trying to scratch? (01:39:42): And then, a lot of the Shape Up stuff is kind of when I have something where I think there's an opportunity or I think there's something meaningful there because of what we learned from customers or the job to be done, research, or whatever it was. Now, how do I turn that into something that we can actually go do and ship in a reasonable amount of time? That's the supply side. That's where the Shape Up part fits in. So maybe it just might be cool for people to see a link there.
turns.zh: 有一件事我可以提一下，就是有时候人们找我咨询是因为他们的项目进展不顺，遇到很多困难，缺乏清晰的思路。但根本原因其实是项目初期的输入太不明确，或者……比如我们不清楚什么对客户最重要，不确定价值所在之类的。所以在进入成型阶段之前，我们需要先进行产品战略阶段的思考，思考“真正的问题到底是什么？”（01:39:11）：这也是与产品战略相关的环节。在这个阶段，参考鲍勃·莫埃斯塔（Bob Moesta）关于“待完成工作”（Jobs-to-be-Done）和需求侧研究的相关内容，帮助我们清晰理解核心需求……这就是我在这个阶段会使用的工具。在定义问题之前，我们需要思考：需求是什么？用户在哪里遇到困难？他们真正想要解决的痛点是什么？（01:39:42）：而“成型阶段”（Shape Up）则适用于当我们基于客户反馈、需求侧研究等信息，发现存在机会或有意义的方向后，如何将其转化为可在合理时间内落地并上线的方案。这就是供应侧环节，正是“成型阶段”的用武之地。所以或许让大家看到其中的关联性会很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great plug for a Bob Moesta episode. We talked in-depth about the Jobs-to-be-Done framework and how to actually apply it. What's the book you'd recommend there? It sounds like basically it's like Shape Up plus this book gives you a lot.
turns.zh: 这对鲍勃·莫埃斯塔那期节目是个很好的推荐。我们深入探讨了“待完成工作”框架及其应用。您推荐的书是哪本？听起来像是《成型》（Shape Up）加这本书，内容会更丰富。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Actually, the one that I recommend the most is Demand-Side Sales 101 and it's funny because it's like sales. Especially for a product person, you're like, "I'm the product person, not the sales person." But it's such a good dive into, "What are people really trying to solve?" And getting into that mindset of, "What's the struggle? What's the problem?" I think that's a really good entry point for that.
turns.zh: 实际上，我最推荐的是《需求侧销售101》。有趣的是，它看似是关于销售的，尤其是对产品人员来说，他们会觉得“我是产品经理，不是销售人员”。但深入理解“用户真正想解决什么问题？”以及培养“用户在哪里遇到困难？问题在哪里？”这样的思维模式，是一个很好的切入点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I don't love that title. I feel like you could have done better there with that book's title because-
turns.zh: 是的。我不太喜欢那个书名。感觉书名本可以设计得更吸引人——

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: It's-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: What's interesting about it is that it's very, very pointy for like if you are trying to make progress on sales, then it's this other kind of sales, this demand side sales. So I think maybe it's more for us who are kind of using it for different purposes. Like we're the product people trying to pull something out of it. That it's a little bit less aligned, but it's still useful.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，它对销售人员非常有用，但对我们这些产品人员来说，用途可能更广泛。比如我们想从中提取信息，但两者的契合度没那么高，但仍然有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. But basically it's like the Jobs-to-be-Done book is what-
turns.zh: 是的。但基本上《待完成工作》这本书——

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Yeah. It's kind of like the Jobs-to-be-Done book that's a bit more tactical. If you're really curious about the general spirit of Jobs-to-be-Done, then Competing Against Luck is a really good intro. That's the one that Clay Christensen wrote with a lot of... I think there's a lot of stuff that Bob worked on that's in there. But for a little bit more tactical like, "What's it look like to do the interview? And how to think about the struggling moment?" and stuff like that, this Demand-Side Sales is good for this strategy stuff.
turns.zh: 是的。这有点像《待完成工作》（Jobs-to-be-Done）那本书，但更具操作性。如果你真的想了解《待完成工作》的整体理念，那么《与运气竞争》（Competing Against Luck）是个很好的入门读物。这本书是克莱·克里斯滕森（Clay Christensen）与他人合著的，里面有很多……我觉得鲍勃（Bob）参与的很多内容都被收录其中。但对于更具操作性的内容，比如“如何进行面试？如何应对困境时刻？”之类的，《需求侧销售》（Demand-Side Sales）对这些策略性内容很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And we'll also link to this episode where you could get the gist of it in one hour's time.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们还会在本期节目中附上链接，这样你就能在一小时内了解主要内容。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Oh, that's right. You did... That episode was great by the way. That's... Yeah-
turns.zh: 哦，对了。你确实……那期节目很棒。真是……是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks, Ryan. Thanks, Ryan. Okay. We did it. This was amazing. I think this is going to help so many people-
turns.zh: 谢谢，瑞安。谢谢，瑞安。好的，我们结束了。这太棒了。我觉得这会对很多人有帮助——

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: We got through it.
turns.zh: 我们已经完成了。

turns.en: We're not done yet. Two final questions for you. Where can folks find the book, find you if they want to work with you? Anything else that you want to share? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 还没结束呢。我还有两个最后的问题想问你。如果大家想找你合作，或者想了解更多信息，哪里能找到相关资料？还有其他想分享的吗？听众如何能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Well, they can find me at my website. That's ryansinger.co. I'm also on X on RJS. I'm on LinkedIn. So just reach me there. And how can people be useful to me? I love hearing from people who are having these problems. If you're having these problems where it's like, "Things are dragging," or, "We can't see the end and we're not getting the quality we need," and all this stuff like man. I mean, this is how I learned all this stuff is by talking to people who are in it. So even if it's not clear what's the next step yet. If that problem is real, it would be cool to hear about it. I'd love to chat.
turns.zh: 嗯，可以在我的网站ryansinger.co找到我。我也在X上用RJS这个账号，还有领英。所以可以通过这些平台联系我。听众如何能帮到我呢？我很乐意听到那些正面临这些问题的人的分享。比如“事情进展缓慢”、“看不到尽头”、“达不到预期的质量”之类的问题。这些都是我通过与从业者交流学到的。所以即使你还不清楚下一步该怎么做，但只要问题真实存在，我很乐意听听你的经历，跟你聊聊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Be careful what you wish for about Moesta. He was just on the podcast and he told me he's got over a hundred LinkedIn DMs with people sharing their struggles with their job search. So here you go.
turns.zh: 小心许愿啊，莫埃斯塔（Moesta）刚上过播客，他告诉我，他收到了超过100条领英私信，都是人们分享找工作的困境。所以现在机会来了。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: Oh, yeah. Job moves, that's a big one. I think that's a broad appeal. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，对。工作变动是个大问题。我觉得这对很多人都有吸引力。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That's true. I'm going to ask you to explain that when you do consulting work, just like how does that work? Who's that for? Just because I know that's something else you do.
turns.zh: 是的。确实如此。我想问问你，做咨询工作时是怎样的流程？适合哪些人？因为我知道这也是你做的工作之一。

turns.speaker: Ryan Singer
turns.en: So it basically starts with uh, either often first CPO or CTO often reaches out first. And when it works well is when we actually get them together and then they understand that they need to change something or we have like a head of product and a head of engineering, that kind of a thing. If those two are both seeing eye to eye that there's a problem, then we can start a conversation around, "Okay. So who would be the right people for a pilot team? What are the things that are going on business-wise that could be a good pilot project?" (01:43:41): And then, I can help to figure out like, "How do we actually..." So almost like guiding through, like narrowing down that pilot project framing so that they have the support that it's going to be successful in shaping. And then, coaching the team so that they actually learn those shaping skills so that they can get through a session and come out with much more clarity. Like how do they actually run those sessions. (01:44:03): So it's kind of first working with leadership, "Who do we need to get to do this work? Who are the right people? How do we bring them into a pilot project?" Narrowing down, doing some framing work on the pilot, so it's going to be clearer in the shaping. And then, giving some guidance on how to get through that shaping with some feedback rounds. This is usually a good approach.
turns.zh: 基本上，一开始要么是CPO（首席产品官），要么是CTO（首席技术官）先主动联系对方。合作顺利的时候，通常是我们把他们聚到一起，然后他们意识到需要做出改变——比如，产品负责人和工程负责人要达成共识。如果这两人都认为存在问题，那么我们就可以开始探讨：“好的，那谁会是试点团队的合适人选？从业务角度来看，有哪些项目可能适合作为试点？”（01:43:41）接下来，我会帮助他们理清思路，比如：“我们该如何具体操作……” 这就像是引导他们缩小试点项目的框架范围，确保项目在执行过程中获得支持。然后，我会指导团队掌握试点技能，让他们能顺利完成项目并获得更清晰的方向。比如，如何有效开展试点会议。（01:44:03）首先，要与领导层合作：“我们需要谁来负责这项工作？谁是合适的人选？如何将他们纳入试点项目？”然后，对试点项目进行框架设计，确保在执行过程中思路清晰。最后，通过反馈环节提供指导。这通常是一个行之有效的方法。

turns.zh: 太棒了。如果他们想深入了解，可以在你的网站上找到相关内容吗？

turns.zh: 可以的。
